blocks.prompt: The Star That Walks on Water
blocks.text: A sea star has no bones. It has no blood either. Instead it pumps seawater through its own body. The water goes into hundreds of tiny tube feet under its arms. The water pushes the feet out. That is how a sea star walks. It walks on water, in a way. A sea star has a small eye at the tip of every arm. The eyes cannot see your face. They can only see light and dark. If a sea star loses an arm, it can grow a new one. It takes a long time, but the new arm comes back.

blocks.prompt: Not a Fish at All
blocks.text:
A starfish is not a fish. It has no gills, no fins, no scales, and no backbone. Scientists call it a sea star, and they group it with sea urchins and sand dollars. A fish is not even a close cousin.

Look under a sea star and you will see why it is strange. There is no blood inside it. In place of blood it uses seawater. Water enters through a little sieve plate on top, then travels down channels inside each arm. From those channels, hundreds of tube feet reach out. Each foot is a tiny water balloon with a sticky end. The sea star fills a foot with water to push it out, then empties it to pull it back. Do that with hundreds of feet in order and the sea star walks.

It has no brain. A ring of nerves circles its middle, and each arm can decide things for itself. At the tip of every arm sits an eyespot that reads light and shadow. That is enough to find the shade of a rock, and for a sea star, that is enough.

blocks.prompt: The Stomach That Goes Out to Dinner
blocks.text:
A sea star cannot chew. It has no teeth and no jaws. Its mouth is a small hole in the center of its underside, and it is far too narrow to swallow a mussel whole. So the sea star does something that sounds made up. It turns its stomach inside out and pushes it through its mouth, out into the water, and onto its food.

Watch one hunt a mussel and the whole plan makes sense. The sea star climbs on top of the shell and grips both halves with its tube feet. Each foot is weak. Hundreds of them pulling together are not. The sea star leans back and holds. A mussel can clamp shut for hours, but it gets tired first. When the shell gaps open by less than a millimeter, that is all the sea star needs. Out slides the stomach, thin as wet tissue, into the gap. It wraps the mussel and begins to digest it right there inside its own shell. Later the sea star pulls its stomach back in, and the empty shell drops open.

This is why oyster farmers once hated sea stars. They caught them, chopped them into pieces, and threw the pieces back into the water. It did not work. Some pieces grew into whole new sea stars, and the farmers had made their problem bigger.

Not every piece can do it. An arm on its own usually dies. An arm with a chunk of the central disc still attached is a different story. It can rebuild the missing arms one at a time and become a complete animal again, lopsided for a while, carrying its old long arm behind it. Biologists call that shape a comet.

blocks.prompt: The Star That Holds Up the Shore
blocks.text:
In the early 1960s a young ecologist named Robert Paine walked out onto a rocky shore in Washington State with a crowbar and a plan. The rock was crowded: mussels, barnacles, limpets, chitons, anemones, sponges, seaweeds, and among them a thick purple and orange sea star called Pisaster. Fifteen kinds of animal shared that stretch of shoreline.

Paine's plan was simple and slightly rude. He pried every sea star off one section and threw it into the sea. Then he came back and did it again. And again, month after month, for years, keeping that patch of rock starless while a neighboring patch was left completely alone.

The starless rock did not become a peaceful place. It became a wall of mussels. Freed from the one predator that could eat them, the mussels grew and spread and crowded out nearly everything else. Barnacles were smothered. Seaweeds had nowhere to anchor. The limpets and chitons that grazed those seaweeds left. Within a few years the count of species on that stretch had fallen from fifteen to eight. The untouched patch next door stayed as varied as ever.

Paine had found something that is easy to say and was hard to prove: one species can hold an entire community together, and not because there are many of it. Pisaster was never the most common animal on that shore. It was simply the one eating the animal that would otherwise take everything. Paine called it a keystone species, after the wedge-shaped stone at the top of an arch. Pull the keystone and the arch does not sag. It falls.

The word stuck. Ecologists now look for keystones everywhere: wolves, otters, prairie dogs, fig trees. The idea began with one man, one crowbar, and a starfish he kept throwing into the sea.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Echinoderm, not a fish
Water vascular system instead of blood
Madreporite: the seawater intake
Sunflower star: up to 24 arms
Wasting disease killed billions from 2013
Kelp forests fell when the stars did

blocks.prompt: The Animal Made of Seawater
blocks.text:
Start with what a sea star is not. It is not a fish. It has no gills, no scales, no fins, no backbone, and no close relationship to anything you would order in a restaurant. It belongs to the echinoderms, a group that also holds sea urchins, sand dollars, and sea cucumbers, and that group is built on a body plan so unlike ours that it is worth slowing down for.

A sea star has no heart and no blood. What it has instead is a plumbing system filled with ordinary seawater. Water enters through a small sieve plate on the upper surface, called the madreporite, and runs into a ring canal around the animal's middle, then out along a canal in each arm. Branching off those canals are hundreds of tube feet, each one a muscular sac ending in a soft disc. To take a step, the sea star squeezes water into a foot until it stretches out, plants the disc, releases a chemical glue to hold, then pulls. To let go, it releases a second chemical that unsticks it. There is no brain running any of this. A nerve ring and a nerve cord in each arm coordinate the whole affair, and an arm cut from the animal will keep walking for a while, on its own business, with no body to report to.

The ambition of that design is easy to miss. An ochre sea star gripping a mussel is applying the strength of hundreds of tiny water pistons at once, patiently, for hours. It only needs the shell to gap by a fraction of a millimeter. Through that crack it pushes its own stomach, everted through its mouth, and digests the mussel where it sits.

Now the part that should worry you. In 2013, along the Pacific coast of North America, sea stars began to dissolve. Arms twisted off and crawled away from their own bodies. Sores opened. Within days an animal could collapse into a smear of white tissue. Sea star wasting disease killed billions of animals from Alaska to Mexico across more than twenty species, one of the largest marine wildlife die-offs ever recorded. The sunflower sea star, a giant with up to twenty-four arms and a span close to a meter, was nearly erased and is now listed as critically endangered.

The cause took more than a decade to pin down, and the false starts are instructive. An early study blamed a virus. Later work could not reproduce that finding, and the field went quiet and uncomfortable. In 2025, researchers reported strong evidence for a bacterium, Vibrio pectenicida, after years of careful work with live animals in tanks. Warmer water appears to make outbreaks worse.

What happened next follows directly from Robert Paine's crowbar. Where sunflower stars vanished, the sea urchins they ate multiplied. Urchins graze kelp, and along stretches of the northern California coast, kelp forests that had stood for generations were shaved down to bare rock within a few years. Most of the bull kelp is gone from some regions. An animal with no brain, no heart, and no blood turns out to have been holding up a forest.
